claim: A taxpayer appealing a PVA real property assessment must first request a conference with the property valuation administrator or deputy, held before or during the inspection period.

A taxpayer still aggrieved after the PVA conference may appeal to the county board of assessment appeals by written petition to the county clerk stating reasons, identifying the property and stating the taxpayer's opinion of fair cash value.
The appeal must be filed no later than one workday after the inspection period ends (KRS 133.045); the Department of Revenue may extend conference and filing deadlines by up to 25 days.
The board of assessment appeals holds a public hearing for each taxpayer appeal and fixes the assessment at fair cash value.

A person aggrieved by the board's decision may appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals under KRS 49.220; a taxpayer who skipped the county board or failed to appear cannot appeal directly to the Board of Tax Appeals.

Assessment standard is fair cash value; PVAs commonly use sales comparison for homes. All real property is subject to revaluation every year and each parcel must be physically inspected at least once every four years.
cite: The Assessment Process for Real Property | Department of Revenue

To qualify, a person must be at least 65 during the tax period or classified as totally disabled; the application goes to the local PVA no later than December 31 of the eligible tax year.
The applicant must own and maintain the property as a personal residence; only one exemption per residential unit is allowed.

When title to exempted property is transferred, the owner, executor, trustee or agent must report the transfer to the PVA; the exemption is tied to the owner, not the property, and a new owner must apply if eligible.

Kentucky imposes a real estate transfer tax on the grantor named in the deed of $0.50 for each $500 of value or fraction thereof, based on the value declared in the deed.

The county clerk computes and collects the tax as a prerequisite to accepting the deed for recording, once per transaction, in the county where the deed is recorded; the clerk keeps 5% as a collection fee.

Exempt transfers include between spouses or former spouses as part of a divorce, under a foreclosure proceeding, deed in lieu of foreclosure, sale for delinquent taxes, partition, and between parent and child or grandparent and grandchild for nominal consideration.

Also exempt: transfers solely to provide or release security for a debt, deeds that confirm or correct a recorded deed, and certain transfers to or from a trustee where the grantor is the sole beneficiary.
Tax is computed on actual consideration stated in the deed; for a gift or nominal consideration the tax is based on the estimated open-market price.

Kentucky foreclosure is judicial only; the mortgage holder files suit and a lis pendens, and the homeowner has 20 days to respond.
After judgment, the judgment and order of sale states time, place and terms of sale; the master commissioner holds a public auction at the courthouse.
Before a judicial sale, real property must be appraised under oath by two disinterested housekeepers of the county; if they disagree the officer acts as umpire.

If property sold under a court judgment (other than an execution) does not bring two-thirds of its appraised value, the defendant may redeem within six months of sale by paying the purchase price plus 10% annual interest and reasonable costs.
Where redemption right exists, the purchaser receives an immediate writ of possession and a deed containing a lien in favor of the defendant.
A deficiency judgment is allowed only if the borrower was personally served or appeared in the action; surplus proceeds go first to other lienholders, then the owner, who must claim them.
Judicial sales must also be advertised by newspaper publication stating time, place and terms.

There is no Kentucky estate tax; Kentucky has an inheritance tax on the beneficiary's right to receive property.

Class A beneficiaries (surviving spouse, parent, child, grandchild, sibling and, under the 2026 amendment, nieces and nephews) are exempt from inheritance tax; the 2026 amendment applies to decedents dying on or after January 1, 2026.

Class B beneficiaries get a $1,000 exemption and Class C a $500 exemption.
A return is due within 18 months of death; a 5% discount applies if paid within nine months, and tax over $5,000 may be paid in 10 annual installments.
If all taxable assets pass to exempt beneficiaries and no federal Form 706 is required, an Affidavit of Exemption suffices for closing the estate.

The state and each county, city or taxing district has a lien on assessed property for taxes for 11 years from the date taxes become delinquent.
